answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Ray Bradbury said this in Misha Berson's interview published by The Seattle Times on March 12, 1993. It is an interview remark about reading and culture, not a line established here as dialogue from Fahrenheit 451.

source.excerpt: You don't have to burn books to destroy a culture. Just get people to stop reading them.
trail: Berson's interview ↗ prints both sentences after Bradbury's criticism of TV advertising.
Wikiquote ↗ identifies that interview and subsequent quotation-book circulation.
The later Paris Review interview ↗ supplies context about the novel's book-burning premise, not the origin of this sentence.

author.name: Ray Bradbury
author.heading: About Ray Bradbury
author.bio: Ray Bradbury wrote The Martian Chronicles and Fahrenheit 451, but also wrote about the practical pleasure of writing. In Zen in the Art of Writing, he collected essays urging writers to trust enthusiasm and keep working.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Berson's interview revisited Fahrenheit 451 and the place of reading in a culture filled with television. The actual article ↗ places the remark after Bradbury's criticism of the rapid succession of images in advertisements; the threat he names is disuse as well as suppression.
